definitions.text: Auden felt that, of all novelists, he best understands the role of money

parts.words: Auden felt that, of all novelists, he best understands the role of money
parts.note: a literary general-knowledge clue: W. H. Auden praised one Victorian novelist above all others for his grasp of how money drives his characters

explanation.surface: A quotation of the poet Auden's verdict on which novelist best understood money.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay: the solver needs to know that Auden called the author of the Barsetshire and Palliser novels the novelist who best understood money.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire chronicles is the one Auden singled out for his grasp of money and its social power.

explanation.walkthrough: 'all-American' looks like one adjective, but its two halves give separate pieces, ALL and US.
explanation.definitionFit: A passing, indirect mention of something in a text is exactly what this literary term names.

explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf's novel takes its title from the Ramsay family's long-planned trip out to the coastal beacon.

definitions.text: When it snowed, as rossetti coinage implies

parts.words: When it snowed, as rossetti coinage implies
parts.note: a reference to Dante Gabriel Rossetti translating Villon's line about where the snows of the past have gone, coining a word for 'last year' or 'times past'

explanation.surface: A question of when it snowed, answered by a word the poet Rossetti invented.
explanation.walkthrough: Rossetti coined the word in his translation of Villon's 'Ballade des dames du temps jadis': 'But where are the snows of ...?'
explanation.definitionFit: Rossetti's coinage means time gone by, and in his Villon translation it is the time when the snows of the past fell.

clue.text: One of those whose library was potted at Qmran

definitions.text: One of those whose library was potted at Qmran

parts.words: One of those whose library was potted at Qmran
parts.note: the Dead Sea Scrolls were found stored in clay jars at Qumran, and are often attributed to a Jewish ascetic sect

explanation.surface: Someone whose books were kept in pots at an archaeological site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Qmran' is the OCR's spelling of Qumran, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found in jars; 'potted' means stored in pots.
explanation.definitionFit: The Qumran community that hid the scrolls is traditionally identified with this ascetic Jewish sect, so a member is one of them.

clue.text: Just over fifty to set back understatement

parts.note: LI is 51 in Roman numerals, one more than fifty
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone a little over fifty about to sit back and play things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SET into TES, after TO.
explanation.definitionFit: This rhetorical figure affirms by denying the opposite, as in 'not bad', a classic form of understatement.

clue.text: Neophyte writers without bad habits?

parts.note: having no, so without gives NO
vices are bad habits

explanation.surface: Beginning writers who have not yet picked up bad habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habits' also hints at nuns' robes, since the beginners in a religious order share this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Beginners or newcomers to any craft, including writing, are neophytes.

clue.text: Change and decline in all around he saw

definitions.text: Change and decline in all around he saw

parts.words: Change and decline in all around he saw
parts.note: a nod to the German historian who wrote 'The Decline of the West', seeing cultures rise and decay

explanation.surface: A gloomy observer who saw change and decay everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue echoes the hymn line 'Change and decay in all around I see' and points to the author of 'The Decline of the West'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oswald Spengler's 'Decline of the West' argued that every civilisation passes through growth and inevitable decay.

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is Shaw's description of Kitty, the brothel-keeper whose trade gives the play its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's 'Mrs Warren's Profession' centres on Kitty, the presentable madam described in the quoted stage direction.

clue.text: Sequel to William-Henry Ireland's Confessions?

parts.note: the Shakespeare forger W. H. Ireland published Confessions; what follows a confession in church is forgiveness

explanation.surface: A question about what book followed the forger Ireland's Confessions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sequel' suggests a second book, but here it means what follows confession in a church: the priest's pardon.
explanation.definitionFit: In church practice a confession is followed by the priest's formal pardon of sins.

clue.text: Monocular god takes overdose at home

explanation.surface: A one-eyed deity overdoses while staying at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The Norse chief god gave an eye for wisdom, so 'monocular' identifies him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse All-Father sacrificed one eye at Mimir's well, so he is the one-eyed god.

clue.text: Tragedy accompanying Tennyson at his death

clue.text: Stevenson suggests half of this for plain version

clue.text: Rank that implies a moral bond, thought Nancy Mitford

parts.note: Nancy Mitford edited '... Oblige', on the duties that come with high birth

explanation.surface: Nancy Mitford on high social standing carrying obligations.
explanation.walkthrough: The French phrase whose second word is 'oblige' says that high birth binds one to behave honourably; Mitford's book took the phrase as its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word names the nobility, a social rank that by the proverb obliges good conduct.
